segments.translit: tam evārthaṃ sahajānandarasapūrṇo hi bhusukusiddhācāryaḥ pratipādayati —
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Bhusuku]{p-bhusuku}, filled with the taste of [innate joy]{sahajananda}, sets forth that very meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.27.m1) introduces the song as the siddha master Bhusuku, filled with the taste of innate joy, setting forth "that very meaning", apparently the point of what precedes. A siddha is an accomplished tantric adept.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lhan cig skyes pa'i ros yongs su gang ba, 'completely filled with the taste of the innate', where the Sanskrit has sahajānandarasapūrṇa, 'filled with the taste of innate joy': it has no word for ānanda, 'joy'. Otherwise it agrees (grub pa'i slob dpon b+hu su kus, 'the siddha master Bhusuku').

Munidatta's tam evārtham, 'that very meaning' (cp.27.m1), points back to what precedes, presumably the end of his comment on song 26, which is not in this pack; so I cannot say which meaning he has in mind. Rasa could also be rendered 'nectar' or 'essence'; I chose 'taste', which matches the Tibetan ro.

segments.translit: adharātītyādi | tatra sekapaṭaloktavidhānāt ardharātrau caturthīsandhyāyāṃ prajñājñānābhiṣekadānasamaye vajrasūryaraśminā kamalaṃ uṣṇīṣakamalaṃ vikasitaṃ mama | tasmin samaye dvātriṃ[41][śa]d yoginīti dvātriṃśan nāḍikā bodhicittavahā lalanārasanāvadhūtī | abhedyā[ḥ] sūkṣmarūpādikā boddhavyā[ḥ] | tatra sthāne sravanti | tāsāṃ ānandādisandohenāṅgohnāso 'bhūt (saṃbhūt) |
segments.translation: 'At [midnight]{ardharatri}' and so on. Here, following the rite taught in the [Chapter on Empowerment]{tx-sekapatala}: at midnight, at the [fourth juncture]{caturthi-sandhya}, at the time of conferring the [wisdom-knowledge]{prajnajnana} [empowerment]{abhiseka}, the [lotus]{lotus}, the lotus of my [uṣṇīṣa]{usnisa}, opened through the rays of the [vajra]{vajra} [sun]{surya}. At that time, 'thirty-two [yoginīs]{yogini}' means the thirty-two [channels]{nadi} that carry [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}: [lalanā]{lalana}, [rasanā]{rasana}, [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}; Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā and the rest are to be understood. They flow into that place. Through the abundance of their [joy]{ananda} and the other joys, a thrill arose in the limbs.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.27.m2) sets the song's midnight at the fourth juncture, when the wisdom-knowledge empowerment is conferred by the rite of the Chapter on Empowerment. The lotus is the lotus of the uṣṇīṣa (the crown of the head), opened by the rays of the vajra sun. The thirty-two yoginīs are thirty-two channels carrying bodhicitta, whose joys thrill the limbs.

equations.en: the thirty-two channels (nāḍikā) that carry bodhicitta
the fourth juncture (caturthī sandhyā), the time of conferring the wisdom-knowledge empowerment

flags.note: The channel names. Munidatta (cp.27.m2) names five of the thirty-two channels and adds 'and the rest' (ādikā): lalanā, rasanā, avadhūtī, then abhedyā and sūkṣmarūpā. I give the last two as names, Abhedyā ('indivisible') and Sūkṣmarūpā ('of subtle form'). They could instead be read as descriptions, 'indivisible, subtle in form and so on', the more so since Shastri restores plural visargas (abhedyā[ḥ] … boddhavyā[ḥ]). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transliterates lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtī (la la nA, ra sa nA, a wa d+hU tI) and translates the other two, mi phyed ma ('the indivisible one', with a feminine ending) and phra mo'i gzugs ('subtle form'), followed by la sogs pa, 'and so on', which suits names in a list. Beyond this the pack says nothing about Abhedyā and Sūkṣmarūpā, so I do not identify them further. The Tibetan also has no word for 'channels' (sum cu rtsa gnyis byang chub kyi sems 'bab pa, 'the thirty-two in which bodhicitta flows').

Possible divergence from the draft of line 1b. The draft has 'thirty-two yoginīs, its limbs thrilled', taking tasu as 'its' (the lotus's). Munidatta (cp.27.m2) has tāsām, 'their' (feminine plural: the channels, that is, the yoginīs), and attaches it to the joys: 'through the abundance of their joy … a thrill arose in the limbs'. He does not say whose limbs. If tāsām is his rendering of tasu, he reads it as 'their'. Not harmonized; the draft line is unchanged.

Shastri prints aṅgohnāso 'bhūt with '(saṃbhūt)' after it, apparently a suggested reading with sam-. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has yan lag yang dag par tshim par gyur pa, 'the limbs became fully satisfied': yang dag par is the usual equivalent of sam-, so it supports the reading with sam-. The Tibetan renders ullāsa ('thrill', spelled hn for ll here as in the song's uhnasiu) by tshim, 'satisfied', as it does in its version of line 1b.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nam phyed kyi thun mtshams bzhi la, which can mean 'at the four junctures of midnight' as well as 'at the fourth juncture' (bzhi, not bzhi pa). It also reads rdo rje nyi ma'i 'od zer gyi chu skyes, 'the lotus of the rays of the vajra sun' (genitive gyi), where the Sanskrit has the instrumental 'through the rays'; this may be a slip for gyis.

kamalaṃ uṣṇīṣakamalaṃ vikasitaṃ mama: I take mama with the lotus, 'the lotus of my uṣṇīṣa', as the Tibetan does (bdag gi gtsug tor gyi chu skyes); it could also be 'opened for me'. The first person is Munidatta speaking in the poet's voice (cp.27.m2). 'They flow into that place' (tatra sthāne sravanti) does not say which place; the Tibetan has de'i gnas su 'bab par byed do, 'they make it flow down to that place'.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena sadguruprabhāvam āha —
tasmin kāle tena hetunā sasaharabodhicittacandraḥ | avadhūtīmārgeṇa vajraśikharaṃ gataḥ | sadguruvacanatattvaratnaprabhāvāt sa mayi sahajānandaṃ kathayati |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
citte śaśa[ha]ram ityādi |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he states the power of the true [guru]{guru}. At that time, for that reason, the [moon]{moon}, the moon of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, went by the [path]{marga} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} to the [vajra peak]{vajrasikhara}. Through the power of the [jewel]{ratna} of the [reality]{tattva} of the true guru's words, it tells me of [innate joy]{sahajananda}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: 'The [moon]{moon} in the [mind]{citta}…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.27.m3) takes the refrain as showing the true guru's power: the moon is the moon of bodhicitta, which goes by the avadhūtī's path to the vajra peak; through the jewel, the reality of the true guru's words, it tells the poet of innate joy. He adds a line of Saraha, "the moon in the mind", as Shastri restores it.

equations.en: the reality of the true guru's words

citations.work: a verse of Saraha; Munidatta (cp.27.m3) names only the poet, and I have not identified the work

flags.note: Shastri restores ha in the Saraha quotation that Munidatta cites (cp.27.m3): citte śaśa[ha]ram, 'the moon in the mind'. I translate his text, but the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) does not support the restoration. It renders the quotation sems kyi dbang po'i mda', 'the arrow of the lord of the mind' (dbang po can also mean 'faculty'), where mda', 'arrow', answers to Sanskrit śara, not to śaśahara. In this same segment, and in its versions of lines 2a and 3a, the Tibetan renders the moon ri bong 'dzin (pa), 'hare-holder', so its translators evidently did not read śaśahara here. Their version looks like a construal of the text without ha, citteśaśaram, divided as citta-īśa-śaram, 'the arrow of the mind's lord'; that division is my inference. So the Tibetan is evidence that its source also lacked ha; it does not settle what Saraha wrote, and Shastri's restoration fits Munidatta's context, the moon of bodhicitta.

sa mayi sahajānandaṃ kathayati, 'it tells me of innate joy': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de dag la lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba ston par byed do, 'shows innate joy to them', with de dag la, 'to them', where the Sanskrit has mayi, 'in me, to me'. The Tibetan reads the opening as b+h+rU'i rkang pa dang lhan cig pa'i bla ma'i stobs, 'together with the refrain (bhrū-line), the guru's power', bh for dh as elsewhere.

I take sa, 'it', as the moon of bodhicitta, subject of the preceding sentence, which matches the draft of line 2b, 'through the jewel it tells of the innate'; grammatically it could also be the true guru. Munidatta (cp.27.m3) has sahajānanda, 'innate joy', where the song has ṣahaje, 'the innate', and adds 'to me' (mayi); the Tibetan line 2b has lhan cig skyes pa smra, 'speaks the innate'. He also adds the goal, the vajra peak, which line 2a does not name.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tam evārthaṃ vadati —
cālia ityādi | śaśaharo hi bodhicittam avadhūtīmārgeṇa yat pracalitaṃ sa eva gurusampradāyāt vajraśikharāgre nirvāṇaṃ prabhāsvaraṃ gataṃ | kamalarasaṃ mahāsukha ❌ rasam asyāstīti kamalinī | saiva prakṛtipariśuddhāvadhūtikā nairātmā kamalarasaṃ tam eva bodhicittamahāsukha ❌ rasena kāyavajraṃ prīṇayitvā mahāsukhacakroddeśaṃ vahatīti |
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ —
paha vahante ṇiamara bandhanetyādi |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the same meaning. 'Set moving' and so on. For the [moon]{moon} is [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}: what was set moving along the [path]{marga} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, that very moon, through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, went at the tip of the [vajra peak]{vajrasikhara} into [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, [clear light]{prabhasvara}. She has [lotus nectar]{kamala-rasa}, the nectar of [great bliss]{mahasukha}: so she is the [lotus plant]{kamalini}. She herself, the naturally purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, having gladdened the [vajra]{vajra} of body with the nectar of the great bliss of bodhicitta, carries that very lotus nectar to the region of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}. And so [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says: 'As it flows on the path, the [bond]{bandhana} of one's own mind…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.27.m4) reads the moon as bodhicitta, which through the guru's lineage reaches nirvāṇa, clear light, at the tip of the vajra peak. The lotus plant is "she who has lotus nectar", the nectar of great bliss: Nairātmā (selflessness as a goddess), the purified avadhūtī, who carries that nectar to the wheel of great bliss (a passage Shastri restores).

equations.en: clear light (prabhāsvara), at the tip of the vajra peak
she who has the lotus nectar, the nectar of great bliss: the naturally purified avadhūtī, Nairātmā

citations.work: a verse of Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācāryapāda); the work is not named. Perhaps his Dohākoṣa, which Munidatta quotes by name elsewhere (cp.05.m6, per the glossary entry tx-dohakosa), but that is a guess

flags.note: The two ❌ marks. Each stands after mahāsukha, and between them the printed text has rasam asyāstīti kamalinī | saiva prakṛtipariśuddhāvadhūtikā nairātmā kamalarasaṃ tam eva bodhicittamahāsukha. The pack does not explain the marks; I take them, as my drafting instructions say, to bracket Shastri's restoration of a passage the copyist skipped, his eye jumping from one mahāsukha to the next. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the whole passage, clause by clause: pad+ma'i ro la bde ba chen po'i ro de yod pa'i phyir ro ('because the taste of the lotus has that taste of great bliss' = kamalarasaṃ mahāsukharasam asyāsti), pad+ma can ni de nyid rang bzhin yongs su dag pa a wa d+hU tI pa bdag med ma ('the one with the lotus is that very naturally purified avadhūtī, Nairātmā' = kamalinī saiva prakṛtipariśuddhāvadhūtikā nairātmā), chu skyes kyi ro de nyid byang chub kyi sems bde ba chen po'i ros ('that very taste of the lotus, bodhicitta, by the taste of great bliss' = kamalarasaṃ tam eva bodhicitta-mahāsukharasena). So the manuscript the Tibetan translators used had the passage, and the sense of the restoration is supported; the Tibetan cannot confirm Shastri's exact wording. Two small differences: the Tibetan puts 'the one with the lotus' (kamalinī) at the head of the next sentence, and it separates bodhicitta from mahāsukharasena, making the lotus nectar itself bodhicitta; I keep Shastri's compound.

Other readings of the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): gurusampradāyāt, 'through the guru's lineage', is bla ma'i drin gyis, 'by the guru's kindness', as if guruprasādāt (the glossary records bla ma'i drin for this word elsewhere); vajraśikharāgre, 'at the tip of the vajra peak', is rdo rje'i rtse mo mchog la, 'on the supreme vajra peak', taking agra as 'supreme'; kāyavajraṃ prīṇayitvā, 'having gladdened the vajra of body', is sku rdo rje rgyas pa'i phyir, 'because the vajra body flourishes'; mahāsukhacakroddeśaṃ vahati, 'carries to the region of the wheel of great bliss', is bde ba chen po'i 'khor lor steng du 'bab pa'i phyir, 'because it flows upward into the wheel of great bliss'.

I take kamalarasaṃ tam eva, 'that very lotus nectar', as the object of vahati, 'carries', which answers to the song's 'carries the lotus' (3b); Munidatta (cp.27.m4) does not take up the song's paṇālem̐, 'along the conduit'. The first sentence mixes genders (śaśaharaḥ … bodhicittam … yat … sa eva … gataṃ); I render it as one statement about the moon, bodhicitta.

Kāṇha's verse is Apabhraṃśa and only its opening is cited, so my rendering is tentative: paha, 'path' (Sanskrit patha); vahante, 'as it flows' (or 'carries'); bandhana, 'bond'; ṇiamara is unclear. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rab tu 'bab pas rang sems 'ching, 'flowing forth, it binds one's own mind' (or 'one's own mind is bound'): rang sems, 'one's own mind', suggests a reading ṇiamaṇa (nija-manas) for ṇiamara, and I follow that sense.

The Sanskrit names the poet Kṛṣṇācāryapāda; I use the glossary's Kāṇha. kāyavajra is listed under the glossary entry trivajra, whose English is 'three vajras'; since that does not fit 'the vajra of body', I marked only vajra (see questions).

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena tam evā[41ka]rthaṃ kathayati —
viramānandetyādi | vilakṣaṇacaturthānandaśuddho 'yaṃ viramānandaḥ | yasya yogīndrasyāvagamo guruprasādād aharniśam abhūt sa eva bhagavān vajradharaḥ | dvātriṃśallakṣaṇayukto vyañjanāśītyalaṃkṛtaḥ | anadhigatatattvānām atrāvakāśo na syād iti |
tathā ca davaṛīpādāḥ —
gavāṃ yūtha nyāya ityādi |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he tells the same meaning. 'The [joy of cessation]{viramananda}' and so on. This joy of cessation is purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}, the fourth [joy]{ananda}. The [lord of yogis]{yogindra} in whom understanding has arisen, day and night, through the [grace]{prasada} of the [guru]{guru}, is himself the [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat}, [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}, endowed with the thirty-two marks and adorned with the eighty signs. Those who have not realized [reality]{tattva} would have no place here. And so [Davaṛīpāda]{p-davari} says: 'The maxim of the herd of cows…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.27.m5) says this joy of cessation is purified by vilakṣaṇa, the fourth joy. The lord of yogis who understands it day and night by the guru's grace is himself the Blessed One Vajradhara, bearing a buddha's marks and signs: so he reads the song's "buddha". Those who have not realized reality have no place here.

equations.en: the fourth joy, if the compound is appositional

equations.src: বুধ (budha), rendered স এব ভগবান্ বজ্রধরঃ (sa eva bhagavān vajradharaḥ)
equations.en: the lord of yogis who has understood by the guru's grace: the Blessed One, Vajradhara

citations.work: a verse of Davaṛīpāda (the Tibetan names him rdo rje Da DI zhabs); the work is not named and I have not identified it

flags.note: vilakṣaṇacaturthānandaśuddho 'yaṃ viramānandaḥ can be read 'purified by vilakṣaṇa, the fourth joy' (my choice, matching the draft of line 4a, 'purified by vilakṣaṇa'), 'purified by the fourth joy of vilakṣaṇa', or 'purified by vilakṣaṇa and the fourth joy'. The glossary describes vilakṣaṇa as a moment, not a joy, so the appositional reading is not certain. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), mtshan nyid dang bral ba bzhi pa'i dga' ba dag pa 'di khyad par gyi dga' ba, reads most naturally 'this pure fourth joy, free of characteristics, is the joy of cessation', making the joy of cessation the fourth joy itself and vilakṣaṇa ('free of characteristics') a description of it. It renders viramānanda khyad par gyi dga' ba, 'special joy', as in its version of line 4a.

anadhigatatattvānām atrāvakāśo na syāt, 'those who have not realized reality would have no place here': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'dir de nyid rnams kyi ma rig pa'i skabs med pa'i phyir ro, 'because here there is no room for not knowing the realities', taking anadhigata as ignorance (ma rig pa). The Sanskrit excludes the unrealized; the Tibetan excludes ignorance.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names the author of the quotation rdo rje Da DI zhabs ('Vajra-Ḍaḍī'), where Shastri has Davaṛīpāda, and renders the quotation ba lang khu rig: ba lang is 'cattle'; khu rig is unclear to me (perhaps for khyu, 'herd', with rigs pa, 'principle', which would answer to yūtha-nyāya, but I cannot confirm it). My 'the maxim of the herd of cows' is tentative: only the opening words are cited, and yūtha stands without a case ending.

The glossary entry laksana-vyanjana ('marks and signs') covers dvātriṃśallakṣaṇayukto vyañjanāśītyalaṃkṛtaḥ, but the Sanskrit splits the pair into two phrases, so I could not use the approved English as one unit and left it unmarked (see questions).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena svabodhaṃ draḍhayati —
bhusuku bhaṇai ityādi | bhusukupādo hi vadati | mayā bhusukupādena prajñopāyamelake sahajānandaṃ mahāsukha[ṃ] sadguruprasādāl līlayāvagataṃ | 27 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he makes his own realization firm. '[Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} says' and so on. For Bhusukupāda says: I, Bhusukupāda, in the [union]{mela} of [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, have understood [innate joy]{sahajananda}, [great bliss]{mahasukha}, in [play]{lila}, through the [grace]{prasada} of the true [guru]{guru}. 27.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.27.m6) says that in the last couplet Bhusuku makes his own realization firm: the union in which he understood is the union of wisdom and means, and what he understood, playfully and through the true guru's grace, is innate joy, great bliss.

equations.en: the union of wisdom and means

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyis bdag gis bshad pa ste, 'Bhusukupāda: I have explained', joining vadati and mayā; it has thabs dang shes rab sbyor bas, 'through the joining of means and wisdom' (sbyor ba for melaka, means before wisdom); and it ends khong du chud pas rol pa'o, 'having understood, [he] plays', making play the result of understanding, where the Sanskrit līlayāvagatam has it as the manner of understanding.
The Sanskrit is passive ('by me, Bhusukupāda, … was understood'); I render it in the active first person. The closing '27' is the manuscript's song number, not a folio number.

questions: m4 (cp.27.m4): the pack does not explain the two ❌ marks. I treated the text between them as Shastri's restoration of an eye-skip from mahāsukha to mahāsukha, as my instructions said, and noted that the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the whole passage. Please confirm what the marks mean in Shastri's edition, and whether the edition should mark restored text in the English.

m3 (cp.27.m3): keep Shastri's restored citte śaśa[ha]ram ('the moon in the mind')? The Tibetan has sems kyi dbang po'i mda', 'the arrow of the lord of the mind', which looks like a reading of the text without ha (śara, 'arrow'). I translated Shastri and flagged it.

m2 (cp.27.m2): I gave abhedyā and sūkṣmarūpā as channel names (Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā). Do you want them kept in source form, translated ('the Indivisible', 'Subtle Form'), or read as descriptions of the channels? If the list of thirty-two channels recurs elsewhere, glossary entries may be worth adding; I have not proposed any.
m2 (cp.27.m2) and line 1b: Munidatta's tāsām, 'their' (the yoginīs, that is, the channels), may render the song's tasu, which the draft takes as 'its limbs'. Worth a look when the line is reviewed.

Keep-source-first-gloss terms that first occur in this unit in the commentary: siddha (m1), uṣṇīṣa, bodhicitta, vajra, lalanā, rasanā (m2), Nairātmā (m4). Within the 60-word notes I glossed siddha, uṣṇīṣa and Nairātmā only. Suggested short glosses from the glossary for the rest: bodhicitta, 'mind of awakening', in the tantras also a subtle bodily essence; vajra, the thunderbolt-diamond, emblem of the indestructible; lalanā and rasanā, channels of the subtle body usually described as running left and right of the avadhūtī. Where should these go?
kāyavajra (m4) is listed under trivajra, 'three vajras'. Would you add a variant such as 'vajra of body' to that entry, or give kāyavajra its own entry? I marked only vajra.

laksana-vyanjana, 'marks and signs' (m5): Munidatta (cp.27.m5) splits the pair ('endowed with the thirty-two marks, adorned with the eighty signs'), so the approved English cannot be used as one phrase there. Left unmarked; is a variant wanted?
m5 (cp.27.m5): vilakṣaṇacaturthānanda. I read 'vilakṣaṇa, the fourth joy'; the Tibetan seems to make the joy of cessation itself the fourth joy. Which construal should the woven note follow?
The poet of the m4 quotation is Kṛṣṇācāryapāda in the Sanskrit; I used the glossary's Kāṇha. Is that the house style for commentary quotations?
